q: According to the ASV-based notes, an animal's emotional and behavioural needs are determined by which combination of factors?
o: Environment, species, genetics, personality, prior socialisation, and life experiences
Body condition score, caloric intake, and kennel temperature
Length of stay, adoption demand, and population manager presence
Baseline cortisol, plasma volume, and leukocyte counts
e: The six determinants are environment, species, genetics, personality, prior socialisation, and life experiences, treated as an overlapping, non-hierarchical set.

q: Which statement best captures the relationship between physical and emotional health?
o: Behavioural health is independent of physical disease
Emotional and behavioural health affect physical health, and vice versa
Physical health dictates welfare and renders genetics irrelevant
Emotional factors only matter once disease is resolved
e: Physical and emotional health are bidirectional: each can degrade or support the other.

q: QOL is described as an array of affective states. How are these broadly classified?
o: Active-arousal and passive-avoidance states
Fight-or-flight vectors and somatosensory inputs
Comfort-discomfort and pleasure states
Socially desirable tendencies and predatory drives
e: Affective states are broadly classified along comfort-discomfort and pleasure axes.

q: What general principle determines whether an animal has a higher quality of life?
o: Eliminating all species-typical behaviours in the enclosure
A static baseline cortisol for 17 consecutive days
Relying only on passive human-presence scans
The greater the pleasant and the lesser the unpleasant effects, the higher the QOL
e: More pleasant and fewer unpleasant affective states mean higher QOL; it is a general principle, not a precise formula.

q: Why does the text describe welfare factors as very individual?
o: Because animals of one breed always respond identically to stress
Because an environment that gives one animal pleasure may cause another fear or discomfort
Because behaviour can only be measured by qualitative analysis
Because personality always overrides species traits
e: Needs are individual, so the same environment can be pleasant for one animal and distressing for another.

q: What are the three pillars of staff competency required of all relevant personnel?
o: Read body language, describe behaviour objectively, and interpret and respond to it
Squeeze-cage mechanics, control-pole maintenance, and fight-kit inventory
Psychopharmacological dosing, body condition scoring, and intake scheduling
Open-ended questioning, active listening, and social-desirability management
e: Personnel must read body language, describe it objectively, and interpret and respond to modify care or handling.

q: Which is an objective behavioural description rather than an anthropomorphic label?
o: The dog is acting spiteful because it missed its walk
The cat is furious and planning to attack the next handler
The dog is cowering in the back corner with its tail tucked below the pelvic midline
The kitten is feeling sad about its environment
e: Objective notes describe observable posture and action; spiteful, furious, and sad are anthropomorphic interpretations.

q: Why must all relevant personnel, not only behaviour specialists, be trained to interpret and respond to behaviour?
o: So daily routines can be disrupted randomly without stress
To let care volunteers administer behaviour medications
To remove the need for objective behaviour records
So that every interaction any staff member has with an animal protects its QOL
e: Welfare is protected only if every interaction, by any staff member, is informed by accurate reading and response.

q: A shelter dog has undiagnosed chronic pain. How does this physical state affect its behavioural or emotional health?
o: No effect, since emotional health depends only on enrichment
It degrades its affective state, because physical and emotional health are interconnected
It freezes its personality until a training hierarchy is applied
It improves pleasure states by prompting more human contact
e: Through the bidirectional link, chronic pain degrades affective state and overall welfare.

q: What operational standard does the text set for QOL, despite QOL being hard to define?
o: Every attempt must be made to sustain QOL for shelter animals
QOL is optional and subordinate to medical treatment
QOL monitoring stops after a two-week stay
QOL is assessed only by outside consultants
e: Sustaining QOL is a non-negotiable mandate even though QOL, like happiness, is hard to define universally.

q: Which set correctly lists the Five Freedoms?
o: Nutrition, environment, health, opportunity, and mental state
The freedoms to hunt, roam, breed, socialise, and rest
Freedom from hunger and thirst; from discomfort; from pain, injury, or disease; to express normal behaviour; and from fear and distress
Unacceptable, must, should, ideal, and exemplary
e: The Five Freedoms are from hunger and thirst, from discomfort, from pain, injury, or disease, to express normal behaviour, and from fear and distress.

q: What is the main limitation of the Five Freedoms that prompted a newer model?
o: They apply only to dogs
They require expensive equipment to measure
They are too numerous to remember
They focus on avoiding negative experiences, so positive welfare is also needed for a life worth living
e: The Five Freedoms emphasise avoiding harm; promoting positive experiences is also essential, which the Five Domains addresses.

q: What are the five domains in the Five Domains model?
o: Nutrition, Environment, Health, Opportunity, and Mental State
Hunger, Hydration, Hygiene, Happiness, and Mobility
Genetics, Species, Personality, Socialisation, and Experience
Intake, Housing, Medical, Behaviour, and Outcome
e: The domains are Nutrition, Environment, Health, Opportunity (agency), and Mental State.

q: How are the domains structured in the Five Domains model?
o: All five domains are independent and equally weighted
The four functional domains (nutrition, environment, health, opportunity) inform the mental-state domain, which determines overall welfare
Mental state is irrelevant once the physical domains are met
Welfare is the average of the first four domains only
e: The functional domains feed into mental state, and mental state determines the overall welfare status.

q: What two things does the Five Domains model add beyond the Five Freedoms?
o: A legal mandate and a fixed scoring rubric
A species list and an age cutoff
A spectrum per domain (including positive experiences), and the insight that positive welfare can exist with an unmet need while negative welfare can arise from a single unmet need
A requirement for daily cortisol sampling
e: It adds a positive-to-negative spectrum per domain and shows welfare can tip either way from a single domain.

q: Which scenario is the ASV example of net-positive welfare despite an unmet need?
o: A dog left in a barren kennel with food only
A cat denied any veterinary care
A group of cats in a chaotic, unpredictable ward
A stray cat on cage rest with a healing pelvic fracture that is appropriately treated and housed in an enriched foster home
e: Despite restricted agency and pain, appropriate treatment and an enriched foster can yield net-positive welfare.

q: Which scenario is the ASV example of net-negative welfare from a single unmet need?
o: A well-fed, physically healthy dog confined long-term to a kennel with restricted agency
A cat with daily enrichment and choice
A dog in a well-run playgroup
A kitten socialised with its littermates
e: Restricted agency alone, in long-term kennelling, can produce profound distress and net-negative welfare.

q: What does the Opportunity domain primarily capture?
o: Caloric intake and hydration
Disinfectant choice and contact times
Choice of environment and interaction, behavioural variety such as play and foraging, and novelty, reflecting agency
Staff scheduling and rounds order
e: Opportunity is about agency: choice, behavioural variety, and novelty.

q: What is the ASV ranking format for its key statements?
o: Low, medium, high, critical
Unacceptable, must, should, ideal
Optional, preferred, mandatory, legal
Bronze, silver, gold, platinum
e: ASV statements are ranked unacceptable, must, should, and ideal.

q: How do the ASV terms must and should differ?
o: Must applies to cats and should to dogs
They are interchangeable
Must means optional; should means required by law
Must is necessary for humane care; should is strongly recommended and expected in most circumstances
e: Must is required for humane care; should is strongly recommended with expected compliance in most situations.

q: How does a behaviour assessment differ from a behaviour evaluation?
o: Assessment is ongoing observation and interpretation across the stay; evaluation is a structured test battery of subtests (for example SAFER)
They are the same process
Assessment is a one-time test; evaluation is continuous
Evaluation is done only by volunteers; assessment only by veterinarians
e: Assessment is the ongoing, interpretive process; evaluation is a formal, structured subtest battery.

q: When is behavioural information about a newly admitted animal most reliable?
o: Within the first hour of arrival
Only during sleep
After acute intake stress has settled, rather than in the first 24 to 48 hours
Never, as shelter behaviour is meaningless
e: Acute intake stress distorts behaviour, so early testing in the first 24 to 48 hours is unreliable.

q: How is Capacity for Care defined?
o: The maximum number of cages a building can physically hold
The total resources needed to promote positive welfare, as described by the Five Domains, for all animals in or coming into care
The number of staff on the daily rounds team
The square footage of the adoption floor
e: Capacity for Care is resource-based and welfare-based, defined through the Five Domains for the whole population.

q: What does the HHHHHMM (Villalobos Pawspice) scale assess?
o: Intake throughput and length of stay
Disinfectant efficacy across surfaces
Genetic predisposition to disease
End-of-life quality of life, scoring Hurt, Hunger, Hydration, Hygiene, Happiness, Mobility, and More good days than bad
e: HHHHHMM is an end-of-life QOL scale scoring those seven items, each out of 10.

q: An animal shows a prolonged, severe negative emotional state that cannot be mitigated. What does the mandate to sustain QOL imply?
o: The care or outcome pathway must be re-evaluated, and euthanasia may be appropriate to prevent unresolvable suffering
The shelter is meeting guidelines simply by continuing to house the animal
Staff should stop recording objective behaviour to reduce distress
The animal should be co-housed with an aggressive companion
e: Unresolvable, profound compromise of QOL requires reconsidering the outcome pathway, including euthanasia to prevent suffering.

q: Which QOL tool is the end-of-life scale, and how does it relate to McMillan's work?
o: McMillan is the end-of-life scale; HHHHHMM is unrelated
Both are identical end-of-life scales
HHHHHMM (Villalobos) is the end-of-life scale, distinct from McMillan's broader mental-wellness framework
Neither is used for animals
e: HHHHHMM (Villalobos) targets end-of-life QOL; McMillan's framework is a broader mental-wellness model.

q: Why must shelter staff record behaviour objectively rather than with anthropomorphic labels?
o: To make the records longer
So that observations can be interpreted and acted on consistently by anyone reading the record
Because subjective labels are faster to write
To avoid training staff at all
e: Objective, factual descriptions preserve data integrity so any team member can interpret and respond consistently.

q: Why is the absence of physical disease insufficient to judge an animal's welfare?
o: Because disease has no effect on behaviour
Because welfare is broad, complex, and heavily comprised of emotional and affective factors
Because the Five Domains exclude physical health
Because emotional factors are purely genetic
e: Welfare includes affective experience; a disease-free animal can still have poor welfare.

q: In which additional context is the Five Domains model now applied?
o: As a framework for assessment in animal cruelty and neglect legal cases
As a vaccine scheduling tool
As a disinfectant selection chart
As a transport route planner
e: The Five Domains model is increasingly used as a welfare-assessment framework in animal legal cases.

q: Why are pleasure states, not just the absence of discomfort, considered necessary for QOL?
o: Because pleasure states reduce length of stay automatically
Because they are the only measurable metric
Because they prevent physical disease directly
Because the mere absence of discomfort is insufficient for an optimal mental state
e: A life worth living requires positive experiences, not just the removal of negatives, which is the core advance of the Five Domains.

q: A shelter dog that was highly reactive on intake now lies flat in the back of the cage and does not respond when approached. A volunteer reports the dog has settled in. What is the correct interpretation?
o: The dog has habituated normally and welfare has improved
The dog is demonstrating a polite decline posture indicating readiness for adoption
This may represent behavioural depression or learned helplessness, and welfare has likely deteriorated
Lying flat with no response is normal for shelter dogs after 48 hours
e: A sudden transition from reactive to non-responsive is not settling — it is a welfare deterioration signal consistent with learned helplessness or behavioural depression. Positive engagement indicators must be tracked alongside absence of reactive behaviour.

q: Which behavioural observation is the most reliable real-time indicator of positive welfare in a shelter cat?
o: Hiding in the hide box for most of the day
Absence of vocalisation for more than 24 hours
Voluntary food intake and willingness to approach familiar staff for interaction
Lateral sleeping position during the first four hours post-intake
e: Voluntary appetite and social responsiveness are positive welfare indicators. Hiding and silence indicate coping or stress, not positive welfare.

q: A cat has been stereotypically pacing the back of its cage for three days. What does this behaviour indicate, and what is the most appropriate initial response?
o: Normal exploratory behaviour; this resolves within one week without intervention
Excess energy from overfeeding; decrease caloric intake
A positive-valence play behaviour directed at the cage door; no action required
Chronic stress or frustration exceeding the animal's coping capacity; initiate welfare review, provide enrichment, and consider environment change or foster placement
e: Stereotypies are not shelter boredom — they indicate that chronic stress or frustration has exceeded coping resources, and welfare intervention is required.

q: Which statement best illustrates the principle that absence of negative indicators does not equal good welfare?
o: A cat that hisses when approached is showing acceptable defensive communication
A dog that stops pacing and becomes non-responsive after five days may be deteriorating, not improving
A dog that barks on the first day of arrival has poor welfare
All animals that consume their full ration have good welfare
e: Behavioural depression produces apparent calm that masks welfare deterioration. Monitoring positive indicators including appetite, play, and social engagement is essential alongside tracking negative behaviours.
